title: All Things Are our Teacher
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett's main teaching is that true freedom and happiness come not from trying to fix or avoid life's challenges, but from creating space for transformation to occur. This involves letting go of attachments and aversions, cultivating a sense of neutrality and openness, and embracing the present moment with an open heart and mind. By doing so, we can learn from difficult experiences, find freedom in our relationships with others, and discover a deeper sense of purpose and responsibility in our lives.

sentences.text: *[unclear: "Once your past penetrating in perfect dharma"] is rarely met with, having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
I picked this title because all things are a teacher.
For some reason I had a pretty hard time coming up with a talk, so we'll see how it goes.
Because part of me feels like there are some really simple and foundational things that we would like to share with the broader community.
They're pretty small but important things, important ways we can work with our hearts and work with our minds, and simple practices of meditation and mindfulness that really make a difference.
They're almost so simple it's embarrassing, and you wouldn't think they would work, but we've tried them.
We've given them a thorough clinical trial for 20, 30 years and they work.
So part of me feels like I could just say that, and maybe in five minutes that would be plenty.
But then I always want to say more.
I want to try to understand how my heart works.
How am I happy and how am I stuck, and how does this human life go, and can I say anything that would help your human life?
The more I think about that, the more complicated it gets and the more confusing, because we have this powerful desire to understand our life, right?
We want to really feel and understand the shape of our life and have it make sense.
So I sit down with my computer in the middle of the night and try to write these talks, try to make sense of life and say something helpful, and I think it's just getting harder to do that.

Maybe the gig with this kind of thing is that, it sounds a little cliché, but I think it's true, the more you pay attention, the more you learn, the more subtle and nuanced and a little bit confusing this life is.
Our parents and our grade school teachers somehow led us to believe it was going to be sort of simple after a certain point, but it seems not to be actually the case.
So I'll try to say something about all things are our teacher, but I wanted to say that little preamble so I feel a little bit off the hook, and I could just give my talk.
You would know that I don't know, and I have confidence that you don't know either, so we're okay.
Or maybe you do know.
Does someone like to take over?
Well, this phrase I picked, all things are our teacher, is adapted from Zen ordination rituals.
Through Zen Buddhism, I and the people here and other places who practice it inherit some phrases and some ritual motions and a sort of container of understanding which then we try to inhabit.
One of the most powerful rituals is an ordination ritual, and we have priest ordinations like every other religion.
We also have a sort of lay initiation that revolves around ethical conduct.

We have an ethics ceremony, which I think is one of the great things that Zen can share with the world: a powerful, ritually empowered way of engaging with our life as moral conduct, as ethical conduct.
Like all religions, we have a list of guidelines and rules and things, but it's given to us in a powerful ceremony.
You study it and then it's given to you.
And in that ceremony, it says:
*From now on, enlightenment is your teacher.
Buddha is your teacher.
All being is your teacher.*
It says being singular.
*All being is your teacher.
Do not put another head on top of your own.
This is the path of mercy for all existence and things.* It's a famous phrase in there.
Isn't that interesting?
Do not put another head on top of your own.
So, all things are our teacher.
Firstly, there are some obvious implications that we all think about, which is that when stuff happens and seemingly happens to us, how do we respond?
Can we work with that response?
Can we turn that response in some way into an opportunity for learning, an opportunity for growth?
Let's just take a minute now, individually, and think about what comes to mind right away.
What's something that happened to you recently that you did not like?
Because those are often fertile ground.
What's something that happened to you recently that you did not like?
Did anything come to mind?
There seems to usually be a pretty good collection of things that we did not like.
And then think, well, how did you respond to that?
It could be something minor, and sometimes minor things are the most interesting because you can work with them.
It could be something minor that just got into your skin.
Or maybe something major happened to you recently or a long time ago, and it's still the first thing that comes to mind.
Some really difficult thing happened.
How did you interact with that experience?
One thing right away is we notice that everything is just experience.
We conventionally tell ourselves, so and so did something to me, or such and such happened, but it's always a simplification in a story after the fact.
So when we're remembering this thing we didn't like, let's try to reflect: what was the actual experience?
Not just the story, if you can remember.
There are secondary experiences, right?
Something happens, you respond to it, and then you have a response to your own response.
Like, "Oh, my God, I can't believe I said that, it's terrible."
Or, "Why?
What's wrong with her?
How could she do that?"
If you reflect on your experience, usually we try to find some way to sew it all up in the end, to make sense of it and move on.

Now, I think this phrase, all things are our teacher, suggests that there's always something we can learn, always something that is being offered to us, even when we don't like it, even including the most incomprehensible and difficult situations that we face.
Bringing up this phrase all by itself can be helpful.
We can bring up the phrase with our reactivity, with our excitement, with whatever it is, and think to ourselves, all things are our teacher, and see what happens.

Sometimes it's obvious that there are things we can learn from difficult situations: conventional pointers for how to live and how to avoid trouble and how to help people and how to be a little bit nicer.
That's great.
But sometimes it really doesn't seem that way.
You may just feel like, no, it's just a disaster.
There's nothing to learn from that.
Or, that was just his fault, my conduct was exemplary, there's nothing to learn from that.

But sometimes if you can stay with your experience, bringing up this possibility, allowing the space in your heart for this possibility, then even if you don't see a thing to learn, maybe there is something.
Not beating yourself up and micromanaging your mind, like, "What's wrong with me?
I can't think of something to learn.
I need to write something down."
But you just open the space.
Maybe the teaching is more of a feeling, not even something that can be verbalized or thought about.
Maybe all things are our teacher suggests more of a sense of possibility.
An inkling in the corner of our mind, something we see out of the edge of our eye, a feeling of spaciousness that we didn't realize was possible within that kind of situation.
Sometimes shifts in the heart happen in ways that we don't really understand.
So I want to recommend the practice of phrases like this that can really operate in that way.
But something like all things are our teacher can only really function if there's space in our life.
Our human life seems not to be mechanical, even though we kind of wish it was.
Science kind of wishes that our life was mechanical.

It would be nice if we could fix our problems just like fixing a machine, with the right teachings or the right practices or the right therapies, or by picking the right friends or the right spouses or getting the right job, all the things that we're always trying to do.
Maybe it would be nice if that could just fix things up, but it seems to be more subtle than that.
You may notice that there are times in your life when you're too busy, too overwhelmed, too caught up or too distracted, and it feels like there's no space to turn around.
Things loom much larger.
When there's no space, it's hard for something like all things are our teacher to operate.
When there's no space, that just becomes one more thing, you know what I mean?
One more project.
"Gosh, I forgot about all things are our teacher today.
I forgot this and I didn't do that, and I'm really stressed out about the meeting tomorrow," and so on.
So what we're finding in Buddhist practice in America is that we can't exactly fix our heart, but we can make effort to create space.
In that space, transformation really is possible.
In that space, phrases and turning words and teachings really can make a difference.
So I think it's really true that part of our responsibility, if we want to be happier and more connected human beings, is to take care of that space.
It's to operate our lives so that we have a little bit of room.
You are all obviously doing that.
You had two hours to blow on a Buddhist lecture, so that's fantastic.
That's great.
And I'm sure you're also using your time in other wise ways.
There are many ways to maintain the space.
One way that we all probably can work on is simply not being so busy, and looking at the causes and conditions that impel us towards our busyness.
It's a powerful shared story that we have, right?
That it's absolutely inevitable to be too busy.
Don't you think?
Isn't it absolutely inevitable that you're going to be too busy?
We all believe that and we tell each other that all the time.
When you run into somebody in the store and you ask them, "Oh, how's work going?
How's this going?" it would be kind of strange if they said, "Oh, I'm really relaxed.
I'm not too busy."
You would be like, what?
What you expect them to say is, "Oh, it's going fine.
I'm a bit too busy," right?
That's what we expect, and we reinforce it in each other.
So why is that?
We might want to look at that as a society.
So it helps not to be so busy.
But also there are some kinds of doing that do seem to help with this.
Meditation practice definitely helps with this.
I'm sure that prayer or regular walks in the woods or doing some kind of creative work with a good spirit, there are a lot of things that can help.
We all have some sense of what helps me hold the space.
Maybe we're also all curious to see what the other possibilities are for doing that in my life, or else why would we be here?
But meditation does have some advantages, so I want to make a little plug for meditation.
The first advantage of meditation is it's really simple to do.
There's very little equipment needed.
We have these elegant looking sets of cushions that cost about 80 bucks, but a couch cushion is fine.
You don't even need that.
All you really need for meditation is a human body, and breathing is useful too, if you're still breathing.
So it's very simple.
You don't need much equipment.
Initially you just need very simple introductory instructions.
You don't need to go to school.
You don't need to get a doctorate in meditation for it to be useful to you.
This simplicity, I think, may be a bit of a barrier for us.

We basically think that since our life is so complicated and our problems are so complicated, whatever the solution might be, it's got to be even more complicated in order to surround all that complicatedness with a strong enough net to hold it in.
But somehow the simplicity of meditation can cut through all that complication.
I think the reason why is that meditation practice allows us to reunite with our own being.
And what could be simpler than that?
To just be, with nothing extra going on.
To take an actual break from our busyness and our fixing and our figuring things out.
So let that go for a bit, and just be a person.
Just be a human being.
We can add many high falutin words to this experience if we want.
Maybe this is connecting with our natural awakened nature.
Or maybe it's being able to be in a relationship to God.
Or maybe it's any number of words.
But really it's just being.
And it seems, surprisingly to us, because of our conjured idea of how the world works, that if we spend time regularly just being, that spaciousness is there.
And there is a kind of natural healing and opening process that can happen.
Within that space, it can be skillful to add some teaching, like all things are our teacher, and just see what that is.
See how that functions for ourselves.
Instead of just talking about it, we should try that for a minute.
Would that be a good idea?
You've been sitting there for a little while already.
One thing I want to make a point about with meditation is that it's not actually a mental process.
You would think so.
You would think meditation would be a mental process, but it turns out to be a whole body-mind process that includes all of our physicality.
So let's stand up for a moment, just right where you are.
It is helpful for you to feel the body.
Sit down on our cushion or our chair.
It's nice in the chair to sit a little bit forward, not to lean so much against the back, and to plant the feet parallel on the floor.
If you want to sit on a cushion, it's helpful to sit on the front of the cushion.
Then it's helpful to tilt the pelvis forward just a little bit.
Make a little bit of an arch in the low back, which just supports the back in a natural S curve.
And in inhalation, let's notice our spine, the backbone of everything, holds us up.
Maybe we could let the spine be gently a little bit longer, don't force it.
Just inhaling a little bit of length and openness.
And then exhaling, just letting go of tension.
Maybe there's tension in the shoulders.
A little openness, exhaling, noticing tension, and just releasing it down into the earth.
Letting that exhalation go.
The eyes could be open and gazing downward.
We do have the eyes open, which we find helpful for awareness and presentness, but the eyes closed is fine also.

Once we've established a little feeling of openness and relaxed feeling in the body, let's see if we can just be simply present with the breathing and the body, just noticing the breathing coming and going.
When thoughts arise, we notice I'm thinking, but then we just gently return our awareness to the present moment with this helpful tool of the breathing.
If we hear a sound or see a sight, we can do the same thing.
Notice that we are having a sensation and just return to awareness of breathing in the body.
It's very simple.

And if there is some secondary drama going on about whether we're good at this or bad at it, or whether our neighbor is probably really good at it or something, we can notice that too and also just return to awareness of the breathing in the body.
Okay, let's try this maybe for three or four minutes.
I'll ring a bell.
You can listen to the bell.
It's very peaceful to listen to the bell.
And then I'll ring the bell again when we are ready to stop.
How about we'll try that.
And you were sitting so quietly before the talk too.
Isn't that nice, to get to be with a group of people and just sit quietly and sort of liberated from, like, chit chat?
That's the other thing that little by little we're learning in Zen practice: there are many kinds of silence.
There is a kind of warm, companionable silence that really includes everybody.
There are also many negative kinds of silence too, which we also know about, right?
A few more thoughts from me about all things our teacher, and then after that we'll take a little break.
And some of us, if you would like to stay, could have a little discussion, and I'd be very interested to hear what you think.
Let's see.
I have quite a few more thoughts about things.
Pages of them.
So I'll try to condense it down a little bit.
It always happens.
But one thing is, all things our teacher seems to be a sort of intentional shifting of our relationship to life and our desires.

One of the things that Buddha taught that's pretty clear, that really makes sense, is that our persistent deep desire for things always to be just a little bit different from how they are kills us a lot of trouble.
Which is not to say we should all become passive.
We need to creatively engage in working with our life and our world.
Buddha taught that too.
But he suggested that it's possible to also be liberated from this niggly feeling that we always, I think, have, if we notice, if we're not too busy.
Oh, that's pretty good, but...
And kind of like our social talk about busyness, we also have the same social talk about our accomplishments, right?
"Yeah, I did pretty good, but..."
And aren't we a little bit that way with everything?
We wish our bodies were a little bit different.
We wish our close friends were maybe just a little bit different.
They're pretty good the way they are, but just a little bit different.
We wish the whole world was a little different or a lot different.
And we certainly wish that there was no death, or maybe a life very well lived according to certain criteria.
At about 93 it would be okay, but other times, no.
We wish that there was no suffering and no trouble and no illness.
And we definitely wish that the things we like would stay around forever.
And permanence is really a bummer for us.
And we wish we could avoid things we don't like.
We wish they would not come into our life.
So I want to toss another phrase in, because last weekend we were studying a 12th century Japanese famous Zen master named Dogen.
And he has a great phrase about that tendency.
He said, "In attachment flowers fall.
In aversion weeds spread."
In attachment flowers fall.
In aversion weeds spread.
So the things that we cling to and really want to not change are like flowers, right?
And the more we cling to them, the more likely we are to have to watch them fall apart.
And then the same in reverse: the things that we really want to avoid seem to just multiply when we go at it with that attitude.
Like there are certain people you'd rather not chat with in the grocery store.
Why do they always go shopping when you go shopping?
It's a law from deep spiritual practice.
But they're there for a reason, yeah.
All things are a teacher, right?
So you hear about these teachings about attachment and aversion and stuff, and it sounds like what they're saying is I'm not supposed to be attached to anything.
Maybe it'd be better if I was just sort of neutral and uninvolved and uninterested in the world, then I wouldn't have any problems.
But that doesn't work.

The antidote to the problems of attachment, and wanting things not to be the way they are, and not wanting to learn from things, seems not to be detachment, but rather loving, loving even more deeply, engaging our life even more deeply.
But seeing if we can release that love from the strings and bindings and conditions.
And we had a literal example of this phrase.
Last weekend we had this big retreat and people came, and maybe some of you were here last week.
And one of the students here noticed that the flowers on the altar were kind of droopy, and she was upset about that and wanted to go to the florist.
And I was tempted to stop her, because we can learn to love drooping flowers, and we need to do that, but she wanted to, and I didn't want to be mean, so she got new flowers.
But there's a way that we can make our life into nothing but running to the florist.
Nothing but fussing and fixing, to try to prop up the sky instead of allowing it to fall with faith that we will be able to get up again.
So all things are our teacher seems to include this understanding that attachment and aversion are another thing that bind us and prevent us from having that space to learn and grow.
And all things our teacher seems to encourage a deep commitment to living our life with what we actually have, to approaching things the way they actually are with full presence.
And recognizing, and meditation helps with this too, that the only room we have, the only place we have to work, is this moment, with this body, with this education, with this situation.
There's kind of no later.
We have this idea of "later I'll be able to deal with such and so, later I'll be able to deal with my mom's problems, because right now..."
But there's no later.
And so all things are our teacher is a radical re-engagement with what's actually happening right now in our life, recognizing that's the only place where we can operate.
And as we study that, we notice that when we're tight and resistant to our life the way it is, there's almost a kind of greed there.
We're trying to hold on to something tightly.
And one of the other things that Buddhism can offer is some suggested antidotes to difficult mental tendencies like greed and tightness and aversion.
What they suggest as the antidote to greed and desire is generosity.
It's generosity.
See, even if we don't feel like it, bring up the practice of being generous, to give more in whatever way we can.
But you know, it's a strange world, right?
The minute you start thinking about how am I going to give more, it gets very complicated.
I was thinking about this because the other day a friend's car suddenly broke in a really weird way.
I don't know if you know much about cars, but her clutch paid.
She had a car with a manual transmission.
The clutch snapped in half.
The mechanic had never seen this before, had never heard of it before.
The clutch plate just snapped in half.
Usually they wear out and other things go wrong, all kinds of things go wrong, but this had never happened before.
And she had to suddenly pay $1,100 to fix her car.
And it made sense to do that.
She had already invested so much in her car.
It was a little painful, I think, to hand over the credit card at that moment.
But she did and drove the car away and tried to forget about it, as we do.

But it just made me think about money and generosity and value and the strange mixed up world we live in, because a few weeks before that my wife and I had sent $500, less than half of that, to an AIDS orphan girl in Kenya, a girl we'd been sponsoring before through a local non-profit, the Slum Doctor program.
We helped this girl get through high school, and she'd done really well in high school and she'd qualify for a university, which is hard to do there, I think.

And the few kids that do qualify for university, it's a little bit subsidized by the state, but they still have to come up with about $500 for a year of college, which sounds like nothing to us. $500 for a year of college.
We're meant to put like $500 every month in our college savings plan for our son, I think, until he's 18.
But it's a huge amount of money for her, of course, so we did that and she's going to be able to go to college, hopefully.
But what makes sense here?
A clutch plate?
Two years of college for a smart, hard-working girl whose parents have died from AIDS?
Do we have to decide that?
How is that all things are our teacher?
How do we learn from that weird situation that we live in?
We a little bit try to avoid how strange and messed up and confusing and not understandable the world is.
Should my friend not have fixed the clutch plate and just sent money to Kenya?
Stuff breaks.
That teaches us too.
Kenyan AIDS orphans work hard or they don't, or they fail or they succeed, or they die too.
How do we respond?
Will we succeed when we respond, or we also fail?
Can we get up again?
All things are our teacher.
So you see, I was having a hard time with this talk.
The more you think about it, the more it's like, what do you do?
How do you live?
How can we let this life teach us and give back?
Because this whole mess is not exactly our fault.
It's not exactly our fault, being born in good circumstances and having things like vehicles that have clutch plates inside them.
I think Mercy Acombo, the girl we're sponsoring, has no ambition to ever own a private vehicle in her lifetime.
That's beyond what she could imagine.
So it's not our fault, but somehow this life is our responsibility.
We are given this body and mind and whatever pile of material possessions comes to us for just a short time, and then it's all gone.
Can we use them well and live in the best way we can?
Can we find a sane and happy way to be guardians of the whole world?
The clutch breaks and we fix it.
The world breaks.
We do our best to fix that too.
But here's the thing that makes this impossible task actually doable, and that is: you can't do it.
You can't do it.
You can't be this separate person over here fixing that world over there.
It's too huge and too impossible.
If we tried to do that, we would just go nuts.
It seems the only way to approach this world, and to really approach all things are our teacher, is if we do it in cooperation with everybody.
I can't do it.
You can't do it, but we can do it.
We can all do it.
So that's why, I don't know if you noticed this, I've been saying all things are our teacher, not all things are my teacher.
There's a huge difference.
And not "I am the teacher of all things" either.

Practicing all things are our teacher brings us back to this massive web of interdependence and support that we actually live in, and we get softer little by little about this abstraction that we carry around called me.
Do I really need to defend me in the same way I thought I did?
Does this me need all these things I thought it did, or does it need different things?
And who is me anyway?
If we look, will we find me?
Am I in my brain?
Am I in my thinking?
Am I in my bones?
Where is me anyway?
But maybe we can learn to let that really be okay and just take the next step.
And I think my last word on this for now is that all things are our teacher seems to fundamentally be a massive expression of trust.
Trusting ourselves to be larger than ourselves.
Trusting our hearts to open to the whole universe.
Knowing that we won't get it right.
Trusting that whatever efforts we make are enough and are just right, and that when we make a mistake, which we will, trusting that too.
All things are our teacher.
Come and explore those questions together here in about five minutes.
We'll have a little question and answer discussion time, and also if you want to come back another time and take up meditation practice, you're very welcome.
You just got most of the introduction already.
It's pretty simple, and there's a lot of literature on the table in the lobby, and there are three or four other meditation centers in town.
Bellingham is amazing in a way.
There's a richness of meditation centers and churches and synagogues, and also forests and beaches and mountains.
We're really blessed.
We have very supportive, really good conditions for practice.
So many people trying their best to be all you can be.
That's probably commercial, but is that the army?
You know what I mean.
And if there's any merit...
Buddhism has this mysterious idea of merit.
So we want to dedicate the merit.
If there's any merit generated from our practice together and our thinking about this this morning, let's give that merit to the people in the world and the beings who need it the most.

The many people suffering today, and I've particularly been thinking of the people in Sumatra, who I think are in terrible shape, and it's kind of slipped out of the headlines, but we might practice generosity towards them and all the other people who need it.
So thank you very much.
Let's please enjoy a five minute break, and if you have time to stick around, I'm very happy to spend another 15 or 20 minutes together and maybe be out of here by 11:15, 11:20.
And if you have a kid downstairs, that's fine.
Shelby's here till 11:30.
And I hope somebody gave Shelby some business.
And do let your friends with kids know it's pretty rare and unusual in the American Buddhist world to have a practice event with child care.
For some reason we're not very good at it, so help us get some traction.
Bring your friends who have kids, and they can come next week or the week after.
All right, so thank you very much for listening.
